title: Route Handlers
summary: **Route Handlers** are `route.ts` files inside `app/` that define HTTP endpoints — you export functions named after methods (`GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, …) that receive a Web `Request` and return a Web `Response` — giving you a real API in the App Router for external clients, webhooks, and any non-React consumer.

subtopics.title: The route.ts file
subtopics.explanation: A Route Handler lives in a `route.ts` (or `route.js`) inside the `app/` directory; its folder path becomes the URL. `app/api/users/route.ts` serves `/api/users`. A segment can have a `page.tsx` OR a `route.ts`, not both, because both own the same path.

subtopics.title: HTTP method exports
subtopics.explanation: You implement an endpoint by exporting async functions named for the HTTP verbs you support: `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH`, `DELETE`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`. A request to an unimplemented method returns 405 automatically. Each function runs on the server only.
subtopics.example:
export async function GET() {}
export async function POST(req) {}

subtopics.title: Web Request & Response
subtopics.explanation: Handlers use the standard Web Platform `Request` and `Response` (and `NextRequest`/`NextResponse` extensions). You read from the `Request` and return a `Response` — the same primitives as Fetch and edge runtimes, so the knowledge is portable.

subtopics.title: Reading body, params & searchParams
subtopics.explanation: Get JSON with `await request.json()` (or `.formData()`/`.text()`), query params via `new URL(request.url).searchParams` or `request.nextUrl.searchParams`, and dynamic route segments from the second argument's `params` (e.g. `app/api/users/[id]/route.ts`).
subtopics.example:
const body = await request.json();
const id = params.id;

subtopics.title: Returning JSON
subtopics.explanation: Return data with `Response.json(data)` or `NextResponse.json(data, { status })`. These set `Content-Type: application/json` for you. Use status codes intentionally (200/201/400/401/404) so clients can react correctly.

subtopics.title: Handlers vs Server Actions vs Server Components
subtopics.explanation: Read data for your own UI in a Server Component (no endpoint needed). Mutate from your own React forms with a Server Action. Reach for a Route Handler when you need a real HTTP endpoint: external/public APIs, webhooks, OAuth callbacks, mobile clients, or non-JSON responses.

subtopics.title: CORS & runtime
subtopics.explanation: Because handlers can be called cross-origin, you set CORS headers yourself (often via an `OPTIONS` handler). Choose the execution environment with `export const runtime = 'edge' | 'nodejs'`, and control caching with `dynamic`/`revalidate` segment config just like pages.

foundations.overview: Route Handlers are how you build HTTP APIs in the App Router. Each `route.ts` maps its folder path to a URL and exports method functions that take a Web `Request` and return a Web `Response`. They replace the old `pages/api` routes and sit alongside Server Components and Server Actions: components and actions cover your own UI's reads and writes, while Route Handlers serve anything that needs a genuine, addressable HTTP endpoint.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Route Handler is a server-only module (route.ts/js) within the app directory that exports one or more async functions named after HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS). Each receives the Web Request (and a context object containing dynamic params) and returns a Web Response (or NextResponse).
foundations.whyItMatters: Not every backend need is a React form. Webhooks, OAuth callbacks, mobile/third-party clients, file downloads, and public APIs all require addressable HTTP endpoints with explicit status codes, headers, and CORS — which is exactly what Route Handlers provide. Knowing when to use them versus actions/components is a core App Router judgment call.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a Route Handler as 'an Express-style endpoint, but file-routed and built on Web standards'. The folder is the URL, the exported verb is the method, the argument is a Web Request, and you must explicitly return a Web Response. If a non-browser/non-React thing needs to talk to your app over HTTP, it's a Route Handler.
foundations.browserPerspective: From the browser these behave like any HTTP endpoint: you can `fetch('/api/...')` from client code, send JSON, read status codes, and (for cross-origin callers) negotiate CORS via preflight OPTIONS requests. The handler itself never runs in the browser.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Stripe/GitHub webhooks, OAuth callback routes, a public/versioned JSON API for a mobile app, image or PDF generation endpoints, health checks, and proxying to internal services while hiding secrets.
foundations.businessImpact: A clean API surface lets external partners, mobile apps, and integrations build against your product, and webhooks/callbacks enable payments and third-party automation — directly enabling revenue features.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Route Handlers give explicit control over methods, status codes, headers, and runtime that Server Actions abstract away; using them only where needed keeps your internal data flow simple while still exposing a real API where required.
foundations.performanceImpact: Handlers can run on the lightweight Edge runtime for low-latency global responses, support streaming responses, and use the same caching levers as pages (dynamic/revalidate) — though by default GET handlers are dynamic unless you opt into caching.
commonUseCases: Webhooks and OAuth/auth callbacks (Stripe, GitHub, etc.)
Public or versioned JSON APIs for mobile/third-party clients
Non-HTML responses: file downloads, image generation, RSS/sitemaps
Proxying to internal services while keeping secrets on the server

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should fetch your own page's data through a route handler.
commonMisconceptions.reality: For your own UI, read directly in a Server Component — calling your own /api route adds a needless round-trip and an extra endpoint to secure.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A folder can have both page.tsx and route.ts.
commonMisconceptions.reality: They both claim the same path, so a segment serves one OR the other, not both.
You set CORS headers yourself, typically including an OPTIONS handler for preflight requests.

config.intro: Follow an HTTP request from URL to JSON response inside a Route Handler.

steps.name: URL → file
steps.detail: The request path maps to a route.ts by folder: /api/users/42 resolves to app/api/users/[id]/route.ts.

steps.name: Method dispatch
steps.detail: Next calls the exported function matching the HTTP verb (GET/POST/…); an unimplemented method returns 405 automatically.

steps.name: Read input
steps.detail: The handler reads the Web Request: await request.json() for the body, searchParams from the URL, and params from the context arg.

steps.name: Do work
steps.detail: On the server it validates input, checks auth, and queries the DB or an upstream service — secrets stay server-side.

steps.name: Return Response
steps.detail: It returns Response.json(data, { status }) (or NextResponse), setting Content-Type and any CORS headers.

steps.name: Client reads it
steps.detail: The caller (browser fetch, mobile app, webhook sender) receives the status + JSON; cross-origin callers first did an OPTIONS preflight.

debuggingLab.title: The browser fetch fails with a CORS / 405 error
debuggingLab.symptom: A cross-origin client POSTs to /api/data and the request is blocked: the preflight gets no CORS headers and OPTIONS returns 405.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: A cross-origin POST with JSON triggers a CORS preflight: the browser sends OPTIONS first. There's no OPTIONS export (so Next returns 405) and the POST response carries no Access-Control-* headers, so the browser blocks the call. Same-origin requests would have worked, masking the bug in dev.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that cross-origin JSON requests need a preflight OPTIONS handler.
Assuming Route Handlers add CORS automatically like some frameworks.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add an OPTIONS handler and CORS headers so the cross-origin POST succeeds.

solution.code:
function App() { const code = [ "// app/api/data/route.ts", "const cors = {", " 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin': '*',", " 'Access-Control-Allow-Methods': 'POST, OPTIONS',", " 'Access-Control-Allow-Headers': 'Content-Type',", "};", "export async function OPTIONS() {", " return new Response(null, { status: 204, headers: cors });", "}", "export async function POST(request) {", " const body = await request.json();", " return Response.json({ ok: true, body }, { headers: cors });", "}", ]; return 
{code.join('\n')}
; }

theory.question: What is a Route Handler and how do you define one in the App Router?
theory.directAnswer: A Route Handler is a server-only API endpoint defined by a `route.ts` file inside the app directory, where the folder path is the URL. You implement it by exporting async functions named after HTTP methods — GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, HEAD, OPTIONS — each receiving a Web Request (and a context with dynamic params) and returning a Web Response. They replace the old pages/api routes and are the App Router way to build HTTP APIs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A file-routed HTTP endpoint built on Web Request/Response.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To expose real HTTP endpoints (APIs, webhooks, callbacks) in the App Router, separate from page rendering.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Next maps the folder to a URL, dispatches to the exported method function, and you read the Request and return a Response.

theory.whyImportant: Building and reasoning about API endpoints is fundamental, and Route Handlers are the modern Next.js mechanism for it.
theory.realWorldExample: app/api/users/route.ts exports GET (list) and POST (create) for /api/users; app/api/users/[id]/route.ts exports GET/PUT/DELETE for a single user.

nestedTopics.title: 405 on missing method
nestedTopics.explanation: Calling a verb you didn't export returns 405 Method Not Allowed automatically.

nestedTopics.title: page vs route
nestedTopics.explanation: A segment can serve a page.tsx or a route.ts, not both.

followUps.question: How do you read a dynamic segment like [id]?
followUps.answer: From the second argument's params object: export async function GET(req, { params }) { params.id }.

theory.question: When should you use a Route Handler versus a Server Action versus a Server Component?
theory.directAnswer: Use a Server Component to READ data for your own UI — fetch directly in the component, no endpoint needed. Use a Server Action to MUTATE from your own React forms/clients without building an API. Use a Route Handler when you need a real, addressable HTTP endpoint for consumers that aren't your React UI: external/public APIs, webhooks, OAuth callbacks, mobile apps, or non-JSON responses like files. The dividing line is 'who is calling and over what protocol'.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three tools for server work with different intended callers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reads, internal mutations, and external HTTP each have an idiomatic mechanism.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Components render server data inline; actions are RPC-style functions for React; handlers are explicit HTTP endpoints with full control over method/status/headers.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrong leads to needless endpoints (fetching your own /api from a component) or missing capabilities (trying to serve a webhook via an action).
theory.realWorldExample: Dashboard data → Server Component; 'create todo' form → Server Action; Stripe webhook and the public mobile API → Route Handlers.

nestedTopics.title: Don't fetch your own API
nestedTopics.explanation: Reading your own /api route from a component is a wasteful extra hop.

nestedTopics.title: Shared logic
nestedTopics.explanation: Actions and handlers can both call one service layer to avoid duplication.

followUps.question: Can a Route Handler do mutations too?
followUps.answer: Yes — POST/PUT/DELETE handlers mutate; you'd use them when the caller needs an HTTP API rather than a React-bound action.

scenario.question: A developer fetches data for a Server Component by calling their own /api/products route handler. Why is that a smell, and what should they do?
scenario.directAnswer: It adds a pointless network hop: the Server Component runs on the server, then makes an HTTP request to another server endpoint in the same app to get data it could read directly. That's extra latency, an extra endpoint to secure, and duplicate caching logic. They should fetch the data source (DB/upstream) directly in the Server Component, and keep the route handler only if an external client genuinely needs that HTTP API.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An unnecessary self-call between server code and its own API.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Carryover habit from client-side data fetching where you must hit an endpoint.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Server Components can query the database or upstream directly, with Next caching the fetch — no internal API needed.

scenario.whyImportant: It's a common App Router anti-pattern that hurts latency and adds attack surface.

nestedTopics.title: Direct data access
nestedTopics.explanation: Call the DB/service in the component; let the Data Cache handle caching.

nestedTopics.title: Keep the API for outsiders
nestedTopics.explanation: Retain the route handler only for genuine external consumers.

followUps.question: What if both the UI and a mobile app need the data?
followUps.answer: Put the logic in a shared service the Server Component calls directly and the route handler calls for the mobile app.

coding.question: Write a Route Handler with GET (list, with a search query) and POST (create, validated) for /api/users.
coding.thoughtProcess: I'll create app/api/users/route.ts. GET reads searchParams from the URL to filter and returns JSON. POST reads the JSON body, validates required fields returning 400 on failure, creates the record, and returns it with 201. I'll use NextResponse.json for both.
coding.lineByLine: GET builds a URL from request.url to read the 'q' searchParam and filters the query, returning the list as JSON (200). POST awaits request.json(), validates that name and email exist and returns 400 with an error otherwise, creates the user, and returns it with status 201. NextResponse.json sets the JSON Content-Type automatically.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) for the list query result; O(1) for the create plus DB cost.

alternativeApproaches.title: Schema validation
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Validate the body with Zod for richer errors.
alternativeApproaches.code:
const parsed = Schema.safeParse(body);
if (!parsed.success) return NextResponse.json(parsed.error, { status: 400 });

alternativeApproaches.title: Web Response
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Use the standard Response.json instead of NextResponse.

followUps.question: How would you add a GET for a single user by id?
followUps.answer: Create app/api/users/[id]/route.ts and read params.id from the second argument: export async function GET(req, { params }) { ... }.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Use Route Handlers for the external/public HTTP surface (APIs, webhooks, callbacks) and keep internal reads in Server Components and internal mutations in Server Actions. Put shared logic in a service layer both handlers and the rest of the app call, so there's one validated, authorized code path. Version public APIs (e.g. /api/v1) for stable contracts.
productionDeepDive.performance: Pick the runtime per handler: 'edge' for low-latency, globally-distributed, lightweight responses; 'nodejs' when you need Node APIs or heavy libraries. Support streaming for large payloads, and apply caching (dynamic/revalidate) deliberately — GET handlers are dynamic by default.
productionDeepDive.security: Handlers are public HTTP endpoints, so authenticate and authorize every request, validate and sanitize all input (body, params, searchParams), verify webhook signatures, and set CORS narrowly rather than '*'. Never leak secrets in responses; keep upstream credentials server-side.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Edge handlers scale globally with low cold-start; Node handlers scale with server/serverless capacity and need DB connection pooling. Rate-limit public endpoints and webhooks, and make webhook processing idempotent to tolerate retries.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Co-locate route.ts with its resource folder, centralize validation schemas and the service layer, and keep handlers thin (parse → validate → authorize → call service → respond). Document the public API contract and status codes.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log each request with method, path, status, and latency; track 4xx/5xx rates per endpoint; trace webhook deliveries and verify signatures. Monitor CORS preflight failures, which often surface as silent client errors.

caseStudies.problem: Needed payment webhooks, OAuth callbacks, and a mobile API alongside a React UI.
caseStudies.solution: Route Handlers for the external HTTP surface, Server Components/Actions for the UI, with shared validated services and signature-verified, idempotent webhooks.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More explicit endpoint code and the need to own auth/CORS/rate-limiting per handler.
caseStudies.lessons: Reserve Route Handlers for genuine HTTP consumers; don't route your own UI's data through them.

keyTakeaways: Route Handlers are route.ts files in app/ that export HTTP-method functions (GET/POST/…) taking a Web Request and returning a Web Response.
The folder path is the URL; a segment serves either a page.tsx or a route.ts, and unimplemented methods auto-return 405.
Read input from the Web Request: await request.json() for the body, searchParams from the URL, and dynamic params from the context argument.
Use Server Components to read your own UI's data and Server Actions to mutate it; reach for Route Handlers when an external/non-React client needs a real HTTP endpoint.
You own CORS (including an OPTIONS handler), runtime (edge/nodejs), auth, validation, and caching — handlers don't add these automatically.
